rows.grounds: that same emission of that power
through the gradual rise of bliss
reaching the clearly manifest power of action
a state that wells up and flows outward

items.question: How is the state of visarga described as it unfolds from bliss into manifest action?
premises: Visarga is the emission belonging to that power.
It arises through the sequential unfolding of bliss.
It culminates in the clearly manifest power of action.
items.inference: Visarga is a surging state in which bliss progressively externalizes as manifest creative action.
uncertainties: asyāḥ may refer to the power just discussed or to consciousness more generally.
items.plain_english: That same emission is visarga: through the gradual rise of bliss it surges forth until it reaches the clearly manifest power of action.

rows.grounds: whose nature draws in that much apparent otherness
like the ocean's unending succession of waves

items.question: What analogy illustrates how visarga contains apparent multiplicity within itself?
premises: Visarga draws in and contains a corresponding measure of apparent otherness.
The ocean appears as an endless succession of waves.
The waves do not exist apart from the ocean's own nature.
items.inference: Visarga is like the ocean: it emits and reabsorbs an endless multiplicity without ceasing to be one.
uncertainties: The exact force of ākṣipta here may be 'drawn in', 'projected', or 'contracted'.
items.plain_english: Visarga itself takes on that much apparent otherness, just as the ocean takes the form of an endless succession of waves.

rows.grounds: this visarga, unmanifest and of the nature of hakala
vocative address to the sacred Kula mystery

items.question: Why is this visarga identified with the principle of desire in the Kula teaching?
premises: The preceding verses established visarga as a surging, wave-like emission.
This emission is unmanifest and has the nature of hakala.
The Kula teaching names this principle kāma-tattva.
items.inference: The creative emission of visarga is the same reality the Kula tradition calls the principle of desire.
uncertainties: hakala is a technical term whose precise phonetic-cosmic sense is compressed here.
items.plain_english: For that very reason, O revered secret of the Kula, this visarga—unmanifest and of the nature of hakala—is called the principle of desire.

rows.grounds: having the form of sound and free of deliberate intention
beyond discursive meditation and focused concentration

items.question: What is the nature of the imperishable sound established in the beloved's throat?
premises: An imperishable, unmanifest reality abides in the beloved's throat.
It has the form of sound yet is without deliberate intention.
It is not reached through meditation or concentration.
items.inference: The supreme imperishable is a spontaneous sound-presence beyond intentional practice.
uncertainties: kāntākaṇṭha may be literal, yogic, or symbolic of the power of speech.
items.plain_english: That imperishable, unmanifest reality, established in the beloved's throat, has the form of sound, is without deliberate intention, and is free from meditation and concentration.

rows.grounds: one brings the whole world under sway simultaneously
in the same way as it is clearly present

items.question: What result follows from settling the mind in that sound, and how does visarga abide in haṃsa?
premises: Settling the mind in that imperishable sound gives mastery over the world all at once.
Visarga has a clear abiding presence in haṃsa.
The haṃsa presence serves as the model for phonemic emanation.
items.inference: The spontaneous sound of visarga, clearly present in haṃsa, is the basis for both mastery and phonemic unfolding.
uncertainties: vaśayet may be read as a general result or as a prescriptive instruction.
items.plain_english: By settling the mind there, one masters the whole world at once; for this reason, visarga abides clearly in haṃsa.

rows.grounds: in the same way, of anuttara and the following principles
in the form of the consonant series from ka to sa

items.question: How does the phonemic emanation from the supreme unfold into the first consonant group?
premises: The abiding of visarga in haṃsa provides the model for phonemic presence.
From anuttara onward the principles abide as the sequence from ka to sa.
The ka-group arises from anuttara as a fivefold emanation.
items.inference: Phonemic emanation begins from the supreme as a clear fivefold unfolding into the ka-class.
uncertainties: The mapping between anuttara and specific phonemic principles is assumed from the tradition.
items.plain_english: In the same way, from the supreme onward the principles abide as the sequence from ka to sa; from anuttara the fivefold ka-group clearly arises.

rows.grounds: by necessity having the nature of the five powers
resting in its own essential form

items.question: How does the fivefold nature appear even within the power of will?
premises: Each emanation is necessarily of the nature of the five powers.
The power of will can abide in its own essential form.
In that self-abiding mode it appears as a single, uniform nature.
items.inference: Even the will-power contains the fivefold structure, though it may appear as one when resting in itself.
uncertainties: The verse is syntactically compressed and continues into the next verse.
items.plain_english: Each case is necessarily of the nature of the five powers; thus, when the power of will abides in its own nature, it appears clearly as one.

rows.grounds: the consonant class beginning with ca
having the nature of the five powers
manifesting in a clear sequential order
through swift operation that partakes of the opacity of the knowable

items.question: How does the ca-group arise from the will-power's movement toward the knowable?
premises: The ca-group is fivefold in nature.
It manifests in a sequential order.
It arises from a power that moves quickly and takes on the stain of the knowable.
items.inference: The ca-group expresses the will-power as it begins to engage sequentially with the domain of the knowable.
uncertainties: The exact referent of yā is carried over from the previous verse's discussion of icchā-śakti.
items.plain_english: The ca-group, fivefold in nature, manifests sequentially; it arises from that power which, through swift activity, partakes of the stain of the knowable.

rows.grounds: from that power in its twofold form
the pair of groups starting with ṭa and ta
but from the unfolding arises the pa-class

items.question: How do the remaining consonant groups arise and complete the manifest universe?
premises: A twofold form of the power gives rise to the ṭa and ta groups.
From unfolding arises the pa-group.
Through this progression the universe reaches completion.
items.inference: The consonant groups map successive phases by which consciousness unfolds and completes the manifest universe.
uncertainties: The identity of the 'twofold' power is inferred from the preceding verse.
items.plain_english: From that twofold power arise the ṭa and ta groups; from unfolding comes the pa-group, because through it the universe is completed.

rows.grounds: this domain having the form of the knowable
extending up to the twenty-fifth element
because it is knowable and clearly manifest
this extent is taught as the form of the sparśa consonants

items.question: Why is the sparśa consonant series identified with the domain of the knowable?
premises: The knowable domain extends up to the twenty-fifth element.
The sparśa consonants are twenty-five in number.
What is knowable is characterized by clear manifestation.
items.inference: The twenty-five sparśa consonants correspond to the fully manifest domain of the knowable.
uncertainties: The correspondence with the twenty-five tattvas is implied rather than stated explicitly.
items.plain_english: Because this knowable domain, extending to the twenty-fifth, is clearly manifest, this much is declared to have the form of the sparśa consonants.

rows.grounds: according to stirred and unstirred states
inclining toward an element of another power
to the nature of the phoneme ya

items.question: How does the will-power give rise to the phoneme ya?
premises: The will-power exists in stirred and unstirred modes.
In a certain condition it turns toward an element of a different power.
This turning produces a distinct phonemic identity.
items.inference: When the will-power inclines toward another power, it manifests as the phoneme ya.
uncertainties: The 'different power' is not named explicitly in this verse.
items.plain_english: The will-power, twofold as stirred and unstirred, turns toward an element of another power and thereby becomes the phoneme ya.

rows.grounds: swiftly assuming the opacity of the knowable
through its inclination toward another power
the nature of the phoneme ra
the nature of the phoneme la

items.question: How do the phonemes ra and la emerge from the same will-power?
premises: The same will-power can quickly take on the stain of the knowable.
It can incline toward a different power.
Different modes of this inclination yield different phonemic forms.
items.inference: The phonemes ra and la are further transformations of the will-power as it engages otherness and the knowable.
uncertainties: The text does not explicitly distinguish which condition yields ra versus la.
items.plain_english: That same power, quickly taking on the stain of the knowable and turning toward another, becomes ra and la.

rows.grounds: in the same way the power of unfolding is twofold
moving toward a power of another kind
the nature of the phoneme va
showering forth the essential flow of creation

items.question: What transformation of the unfolding power produces the phoneme va?
premises: The unfolding power is twofold.
It can move toward a power of a different kind.
The phoneme va is associated with pouring forth the essence of creation.
items.inference: When the unfolding power engages otherness, it becomes va, the phonemic expression of creative outpouring.
uncertainties: The twofold nature of unmeṣa-śakti is not specified in this verse.
items.plain_english: Likewise, the twofold power of unfolding, moving toward a different power, becomes va, which pours forth the essence of creation.

rows.grounds: the will-power itself having reached supreme bliss
fire from illumination and earth from stability

items.question: How do elemental principles arise from modes of the will-power?
premises: The will-power can reach the state of supreme bliss.
Its swiftness, illumination, and firmness are distinct modes.
These modes are named as air, fire, and earth.
items.inference: Elemental principles are expressions of modal qualities within the same will-power.
uncertainties: The verse compresses several identifications into a single compound chain.
items.plain_english: The will-power itself, having reached supreme bliss, is called air through swiftness, fire through shining, and earth through firmness.

rows.grounds: this tetrad is therefore called the inner group
because it is contained within will and the other powers
at the point of its own culmination

items.question: Why is this tetrad called the inner group in the phonemic emanation?
premises: A fourfold group has just been described.
It is contained within will and the other powers.
It abides at the point of their own completion.
items.inference: The tetrad is called inner because it remains internal to the powers and marks their culmination.
uncertainties: The exact members of the tetrad are carried over from the immediately preceding verses.
items.plain_english: This fourfold group is called the inner one because it is contained within will and the other powers and abides at their completion.

rows.grounds: of powers of the same kind, starting with will
this is of the nature of agitation
including those characterized by agitation and non-agitation

items.question: What characterizes the joining of kindred powers in this emanation?
premises: Kindred powers such as will can be joined together.
These powers may be stirred or unstirred.
The tradition describes their joining in a specific way.
items.inference: The conjunction of kindred powers is fundamentally a stirring or agitation within consciousness.
uncertainties: The scope of 'kindred powers' may include more than icchā, jñāna, and kriyā.
items.plain_english: The joining of kindred powers, beginning with will—whether stirred or unstirred—is said to be of the nature of agitation.

rows.grounds: in relation to what is of the same kind
one of those two supreme aspects
if that is for the arising of bliss

items.question: What twofold movement is possible within the supreme itself?
premises: The supreme can relate to what is of the same kind.
This relation takes a twofold course.
One aspect of that twofold supreme can serve the arising of bliss.
items.inference: Even within the supreme there is a twofold movement, one aspect of which gives rise to bliss.
uncertainties: The verse is syntactically incomplete and continues into the next verse.
items.plain_english: In relation to what is of the same kind, the supreme has a twofold movement; if one of those supreme aspects is for the arising of bliss,

rows.grounds: it will be able to produce
yet here too the supreme aspect

items.question: When does the joining within the supreme become a manifest stirring?
premises: One supreme aspect can give rise to bliss.
Its joining produces a clearly manifest stirring.
The second supreme aspect is not by itself sufficient for emanation.
items.inference: Manifest creative stirring arises when the bliss-producing aspect of the supreme enters into conjunction.
uncertainties: The sentence continues into the next verse, so the insufficiency is completed there.
items.plain_english: then, when it is joined, a clearly manifest stirring arises; yet even the second supreme aspect, by itself, is not sufficient for emanation.

rows.grounds: without agitation there remains only the supreme nature
and tinged by the object of willing

items.question: What condition of will appears when stirring is absent or incomplete?
premises: Without stirring, the state remains purely supreme.
Will can be devoid of action.
Will can be tinged by what is to be willed.
items.inference: In the absence of full stirring, will appears either as actionless or as colored by its intended object.
uncertainties: The syntax bridges into the next verse, which names the three resulting states.
items.plain_english: It is not sufficient; without stirring there remains only the supreme nature. Will may be devoid of action, or it may be tinged by what is to be willed.

rows.grounds: as not-yet-opened, opening, and fully opened

items.question: What three states does will assume through swiftness and firmness?
premises: Will is differentiated by swiftness and firmness.
This differentiation produces three conditions.
The tradition names them as unopened, opening, and opened.
items.inference: The will-power unfolds through three graded states of manifestation.
uncertainties: The mapping of swiftness and firmness to each of the three states is not spelled out.
items.plain_english: Divided by swiftness and firmness, it takes on three states: unopened, opening, and fully opened.

rows.grounds: the object as it is being willed
since its essential nature is not lost
by its own inner fervor or potency
through the prompting of its own autonomous nature

items.question: How does the willed object remain threefold without losing its essential nature?
premises: The willed object appears in three modes within will.
Its essential nature does not fall away in these modes.
Its manifestation is driven by its own inner potency and freedom.
items.inference: The threefold manifestation of the willed arises from the same reality through its own autonomous potency.
uncertainties: ūṣman can suggest heat, fervor, or subtle potency; the exact nuance is contextual.
items.plain_english: Within that will the object is threefold, yet its essential nature does not fall away; that same reality, by its own inner potency and the impulse of its own freedom,

rows.grounds: the three sibilants śa, ṣa, sa

items.question: How do the sibilants externalize the universe in manifest form?
premises: The same autonomous potency projects manifestation outward.
This projection appears as the triad of sibilants śa, ṣa, and sa.
In the phoneme sa the universe shines forth clearly.
items.inference: The sibilants, culminating in sa, are the phonemic form in which the universe becomes outwardly manifest.
uncertainties: The distinct roles of śa and ṣa are not differentiated in this verse.
items.plain_english: Making itself external and clearly projected, it abides as the triad śa, ṣa, and sa; and from that very basis the universe shines forth clearly in sa.

rows.grounds: yogins proclaim that to be so
in the pauses at the start and end of agitation

items.question: Where do yogins recognize the supreme immortal abode within the process of stirring?
premises: Stirring has phases of beginning and ending.
There are cessations or pauses at those phases.
Yogins identify that same reality as supreme nectar.
items.inference: The supreme immortal state is directly recognized in the still gaps within the movement of stirring.
uncertainties: The exact experiential referent of 'cessations' may include breath, mantra, or awareness transitions.
items.plain_english: Yogins declare that to be the supreme immortal abode; in the cessations at the beginning and end of stirring, that same reality is the supreme nectar.

rows.grounds: in the hiss of delight, in the feeling of bliss, in being, in absorption, and in samādhi

items.question: In what lived experiences is that same undivided absolute recognized?
premises: The supreme nectar was identified in the pauses of stirring.
It is also recognized in spontaneous experiences of delight, being, absorption, and samādhi.
The tradition names that same reality as the supreme undivided absolute.
items.inference: The same undivided absolute is disclosed both in subtle pauses and in immediate states of blissful absorption.
uncertainties: sītkāra may refer to a literal hiss, a subtle sound, or an ecstatic exhalation.
items.plain_english: In the hiss of delight, in bliss, in pure being, in absorption, and in samādhi, they declare that same reality to be the supreme, undivided absolute.
